qualitative.gate_3m_moat_note: Baker Hughes possesses a defensible installed base of turbomachinery (gas turbines and compressors) in its Industrial & Energy Technology (IET) segment with captive OEM aftermarket service agreements, particularly in global LNG liquefaction infrastructure. However, its Oilfield Services & Equipment (OFSE) segment operates in a cyclical, competitive market alongside SLB and Halliburton where pricing power is tethered to volatile customer capex budgets. Consolidated 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~7.5% and peak-cycle 2024-2025 ROIC of ~10.4-10.6% fail the required 12% cycle-neutral hurdle. Long-term moat erosion threats include the secular energy transition away from upstream hydrocarbons, cyclical E&P capex cuts, and alternative electrification technologies.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Despite leadership in LNG turbomachinery and a large installed base driving aftermarket service annuities, Baker Hughes fails the empirical moat proof with a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~7.5% and peak-cycle ROIC of ~10.4-10.6% (below the 12% threshold). Heavy exposure to cyclical oilfield services (OFSE) dilutes returns and pricing power across full commodity cycles.
qualitative.evidence: Formed in its modern structure via the 2017 GE Oil & Gas combination and subsequent separation, Baker Hughes operates two core segments: Industrial & Energy Technology (IET) and Oilfield Services & Equipment (OFSE). While IET delivers strong order backlogs and higher operating margins (~17-18%) driven by global LNG liquefaction projects and turbomachinery service annuities, OFSE remains cyclical and price-sensitive. 10-year average ROIC is low single digits due to historical write-downs; 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.5%. Despite strong recent FCF generation ($2.3B in 2024, $2.7B in 2025) and trailing ROIC reaching 10.4%-10.6%, returns fail to cross the 12% multi-cycle hurdle.
